chapter_theme: The first twenty-five songs of the Azhuganni Siddhar, each ending in a cry to the Mother (என் கண்ணம்மா!). The poet maps the body as a town in cipher, with its root seat, six houses, five ruling men, twelve-legged horse and needle-point gate, and laments that he cannot hold the breath still, cannot find a medicine to change his birth, and has been undone by love, kin, drugs and his own ignorance; the question he keeps asking is whether he will yet see the Mother's play inside this body.
structure_note: Every song is a கலித்தாழிசை of four lines plus the refrain என் கண்ணம்மா! and a closing question. 1489 to 1494 set out the body-town in cipher; 1495 to 1499 are complaints of the body, its boiling, its filth and its death; 1500 to 1503 picture the inner hunt and the ride; 1504 to 1513 turn to attachment, kin, drugs and the poet's own failure.

1489.reading: In the root seat, in the six houses, in the ornamented seat at the middle of the street of quibbles, in the milk seat where a pillar grew up as fire, and in the seat above: will I not see your play, my Mother?
1489.nuance: The four பதி (seats) with the six houses are read by tradition as the body's centres: மூலம் the root, the six houses the adharas, the pillar grown as fire the coiled power rising in the central channel, the seat above the crown. குதர்க்கத் தெரு, the street of quibbling, is unexplained; it may be the mouth or the restless mind. The Mother's play is the goddess at work in the body.

1490.reading: An eight-span body, fourteen gates, five men who hold the council and two towns; you speak without fear, yet fearing punishment you do not stand firm in the heart and wither beyond your state.
1490.nuance: எண்சாண் உடம்பு, the body eight spans long, is a stock Siddhar measure. ஏழிரண்டு வாயில் is fourteen gates where most texts count nine; some read the fourteen as the nine openings plus five senses. The five panchayat men are taken as the five senses or the five elements, and the two towns as the two eyes or the two breaths. Who is addressed, the soul or the Mother, is unclear.

1491.reading: At the pearl gate in the street of three junctions, spreading the ten petals and seating her on the five-fold couch, holding that steady at an hour when no one is near, will I not light the standing lamp and draw the kolam and look, my Mother?
1491.nuance: முச்சந்தி, where three streets meet, is read as the brow-centre where the three channels join; the ten petals are the lotus of the navel or heart, the five-fold couch the five elements or senses. The lamp and the kolam are a householder's puja turned inward: worship done alone, with the mind held still.

1492.reading: Samba rice is cooked and ready; saying 'you must eat', pouring ghee by the measure, serving rice like pearls with three fruits and sugar, sweet honey-nectar: will I not eat and tire of it, my Mother?
1492.nuance: The plain sense is a feast offered to the Mother or by her. In the cipher the rice, ghee, fruits and honey are the nectar (தேனாமிர்தம்) said to drip from the moon-centre when the breath is held, which the yogi feeds on. தின்று களைப் பாரேனோ, 'eat till I tire', suggests the feeding is endless.

1493.reading: Wearing golden anklets, lifting the ornamented foot, dressed in red-gold cloth, with kohl drawn on her carp eyes and fine gold jewels, in the six-cornered street, seated on the pillar: will I not look at her until my eyes are cooled, my Mother?
1493.nuance: The goddess is dressed as a dancing girl. The six-cornered street (அறுகோண வீதி) is read as the six-petalled or six-angled centre, and the pillar (கம்பம், as in 1489) as the central channel on which she stands. கண்குளிர, with cooled eyes, is the devotee's vision rather than a yogic claim.

1494.reading: A horse that cannot be reached, with twelve legs, a burden even when let go: if I stop it in the street, take a rope and bind all four legs tight, could I not rule all the eight-sided land, my Mother?
1494.nuance: The horse is the breath in Siddhar cipher; its twelve legs are the twelve finger-breadths the breath travels, or the twelve kalas. Binding its four legs is holding the breath, and ruling the eight-sided country (அட்டாள தேசம்) is the sovereignty of the eight siddhis, or of the eight directions. The verse is a single image kept in question form.

1495.reading: My belly boils like a smith's forge; when I say 'stop' I cannot make it stand still; and if I could say 'stop' and hold it still, would not Death, who came saying 'kill', flee with his household, my Mother?
1495.nuance: The boiling belly is read as the breath or the digestive fire that will not be held; the claim is the Siddhar one that holding it drives Death away. The repetition of the line with the condition reversed is the song's usual turn.

1496.reading: A body of filth, a pot in which salt has stood: I cannot get the medicine to be born otherwise; if I could get the medicine to be born otherwise, would I not leave this filthy body and reach your feet, my Mother?
1496.nuance: உப்பிருந்த பாண்டம், a pot that salt has eaten through, makes the body a vessel that corrodes from within. The medicine to change birth (மாற்றிப் பிறக்க மருந்து) can be read as the Siddhar's rejuvenating drug or as the knowledge that ends birth; the verse admits having neither.

1497.reading: Told that eating the banana would hurt my mouth, I ate the pandanus fruit and death came to me; if, leaving the pandanus and dying without dying, I ate the banana, would life not come to me, my Mother?
1497.nuance: The two fruits are a code the verse does not open. Tradition takes the banana as the inner nectar or the true teaching, refused because it seems hard, and the pandanus, fragrant but inedible, as worldly pleasure or false doctrine. சாகாமற் சாக, to die without dying, is the Siddhar death of the ego while the body lives.

1498.reading: Living in the town of the bag, born in the town of the waste, I do not know the Vedanta house by which to go to the town of truth; if I knew it, would not the bag-town and the truth-town both end in the waste, my Mother?
1498.nuance: பையூர் is the womb or the body as a bag, பாழூர் the waste or void, மெய்யூர் the town of truth. The closing line is puzzling: once the house is known, even the truth-town ends in பாழ், which tradition reads as the void beyond both, not as ruin. The verse plays on வீடு as house and as release.

1499.reading: Are you my uncle's daughter or my sister-in-law? I do not know; Kama's arrow burns me like fire. If you became uncle's daughter and sister-in-law to me, would not all Kama's arrows burn up as I open my eyes, my Mother?
1499.nuance: The poet asks what kin the goddess is to him, in the idiom of a village marriage; both relationships are those a man may wed. The cure for lust proposed is union with the Mother herself, which turns Kama's fire back on itself.

1500.reading: Making the sky a bow and the five letters an arrow, mounting the chariot of mantra to hunt the deer, in the grove where the moon and sun have gone, will I not come and play and look with a glad mind, my Mother?
1500.nuance: The deer hunt is the chase of the restless mind (மான் as deer and as the mind). Sun and moon are the two breaths in Siddhar cipher; the grove where they have gone is where the two channels end and the central one opens. The five letters are the Siva mantra.

1501.reading: Riding the wild elephant through the market street, will the townsfolk stop us and laugh? Even if the townsfolk stop us and laugh, will I not ride the wild elephant and see with cooled eyes, my Mother?
1501.nuance: The wild elephant is read as the untamed mind or the breath; riding it in public is the yogi's open indifference to the town's mockery. The verse accepts the ridicule in advance.

1502.reading: Below the crown, inside the needle-point gate, climbing above the loft, taking the sky's blood, twisting the cord of the girdle, on the road to Kayalur I set it down and forgot it, and so I was ruined in every way, my Mother.
1502.nuance: ஊசிமுனை வாசல், the needle-point gate, is the Siddhars' name for the opening of the central channel at the crown. வானுதிரம், the blood of the sky, is read as the nectar or the seed drawn upward. காயலூர் is read as a pun on காயம், the body. The lament is of a practice reached and then lost.

1503.reading: Drawing the bud up with the nose and lifting it as six, spreading the net with the tongue and building a four-square house, spreading the net with the tongue inside the four-square house, I do not see the nose and suffer entirely, my Mother.
1503.nuance: Breath drawn by the nose and the tongue turned back are the pranayama and khechari of yoga; the four-square house is read as the root or the brow. The last line admits the practice failed: he cannot find the nose, that is, the breath itself. மூவிரண்டு, two threes, may be the six centres or the breath's measures.

1504.reading: The thought came to me to strew the flowers of desire; to end the strength of sin I did not get the strength of the bond, and if I had, would not the three flowers of desire stand before my eyes, my Mother?
1504.nuance: பாம வலி is read as பாப வலி, the force of sin, and பாச வலி as the strength of the bond, or of love. The three flowers of desire are unexplained; the three desires for land, gold and women is one traditional gloss. The verse may mean that love's bond, rightly placed, is the cure for lust, but the text is too compressed to be sure.

1505.reading: So that the ... would not show, I fenced a span-wide plot, planted onion seedlings and waited many days; without eating the onion I ate only the trouble above, and so, without the ... showing, I die without dying, my Mother.
1505.nuance: தங்காயம் is unknown; it may be a plant name or a corrupt word. The onion planted and never eaten is read as a practice begun and never brought to fruit. சாகிறண்டி சாகாமல் reverses the Siddhar ideal of dying without death into its failure.

1506.reading: Like moss spreading on water that nothing holds, though I look and look your delusion does not lift; if, looking and looking, your delusion lifted, it would be water with nothing clinging, and would the moss be anything else, my Mother?
1506.nuance: பற்றற்ற நீர் puns on பற்று: water with no attachment, and water with no footing for the moss. The moss is the Mother's own மயக்கம், so delusion and the clear water are not two things; once the delusion lifts, the moss is seen to have been water all along.

1507.reading: The learned and the rest, kin and parents, I took as one with the ninety-six; when kin and parents leave the town, how is it that I stand without any kin, having lost all support?
1507.nuance: The ninety-six are the tattvas of the Saiva count. The verse sets family and the body's constituents together: both are the company that leaves. ஊரைவிட்டுப் போகையிலே, leaving the town, is dying or the dissolution of the tattvas at release.

1508.reading: Below the eye is the nose, at the middle beside the ears; climbing above the uvula there is much of your novelty; even for those who have climbed above the uvula and seen your novelty, below the eye is the nose, my Mother, and there are many reasons.
1508.nuance: உண்ணாக்கு மேலேறி, climbing above the uvula, is the khechari of the yogis, the tongue turned back to the cavity above the palate where the nectar is said to be tasted. The repeated 'below the eye is the nose' keeps the body-map in view; the closing காரணங்கள் மெத்தவுண்டே is deliberately unexplained.

1509.reading: Taking dyeing stuffs, adding cinnabar, mixing a magic powder and pouring civet ghee, she put a dot on the brow between the eyebrows, and by the drug she placed there I came to this guise, my Mother.
1509.nuance: The Mother applies the brow-mark as a drug and the poet is changed by it. The plain reading is a woman's cosmetics turned to a charm; the coded one is the brow-centre (புருவ நடு) opened by the goddess. The formula names real materials, சாதிலிங்கம் and வாலுழுவை நெய், but is not a recipe.

1510.reading: A root from the underworld with arsenic added, with the goblin-drug joined and white-thorn ghee poured, a red vermilion ink that terrifies the whole world: by the drug she gave I burn like a coal, my Mother.
1510.nuance: The verse lists alchemical materials, பாடாணம், வேதாளம், செந்தூரம், as the Mother's drug, and its effect is the poet's burning. Whether the burning is the heat of the awakened power or the ruin of a failed preparation is open; both readings are traditional.

1511.reading: Fear of thieves will not let me lift my foot; a child that stands crying is a burden to the mother who bore it; if the child did not cry and the mother's heart did not ache, would I see even a mustard seed of fear of thieves, my Mother?
1511.nuance: The thieves are the five senses that rob the body in Siddhar idiom; the crying child is the poet himself before the Mother. The verse ties his fear to his own clamour: a quiet child has nothing to fear.

1512.reading: The five kings who rule the town, speaking their valour while they do not part, when they part and separate the town itself is lost; how is it that the warrior kings died?
1512.nuance: The five kings of the body-town are the five elements, or the five senses; their parting is death, which takes the town with them. The question at the end treats their mortality as a surprise, since they were kings.

1513.reading: I am an unfit outcast who talks ignorance; I do not know the undying head, I do not know my own knowledge, I do not know the leg that does not cook; I was ruined by fate and, hurting without being hurt, in a moment I turned to wax, my Mother.
1513.nuance: சாகாத் தலை, வேகாத கால் and போகாத புனல் are the Siddhars' triad of the deathless head, the unburnt leg and the unflowing water, read as the crown, the breath and the seed held still; the poet confesses he knows none of them. புலையன் is self-abuse, not caste. Melting to wax is his collapse before the Mother.

links.note: Both ride the breath as a horse with twelve legs: Tirumular says bind it fast and drink and the body lasts a thousand years; the Azhuganni binds its four legs with a rope and asks whether he could then rule the eight-sided land. The Siddhar keeps the claim in a question.

Tirumular's lord of the five, chief of the town, has a horse to ride to salvation that throws the false; the Azhuganni's horse is a burden even when let go and must be caught in the street. The town and the horse are the same body and breath.

The Azhuganni laments losing the practice at the needle-point gate at the crown; Tirumular says talk of the breath and the needle is useless until desire and attachment are cut. Tirumular names the condition the Siddhar's lament lacks.

Moss on a pond stands for the mind's clouding in both: Tirumular's worshippers have minds like a stone dropped in a mossy pond, without love; the Azhuganni's moss is the Mother's own delusion on clear water, which lifts to leave the water as it was.

Both count the ninety-six under the five: Tirumular's five ministers and their ninety-six who mean to rule, the Azhuganni's ninety-six taken as one with kin and parents. Both treat the body's constituents as a company that must be ruled or will leave.

Tirumular's five ministers rule the body with their ninety-six and exact tribute; the Azhuganni follows the five kings to their death and asks how the warrior kings died, which Tirumular's verse does not reach.

Both put the filthy body beside the Lord's feet and name medicine as what failed: Arunagiri tried worthless medicines and yogas for this ashen body before asking for the feet; the Azhuganni cannot get the medicine to be born otherwise and would leave the body for the Mother's feet if he had it.

Melting wax in both: Tirumular's rising fire works on the body as melting on wax and leads to knowing the mother; the Azhuganni, not knowing the deathless head, melts to wax in a moment before the Mother. The same softening is attainment in one and collapse in the other.

Both pair the five letters with the rising of sun and moon, the two breaths: Tirumular says at that hour none knows the fitting mantra but the five letters can be recited; the Azhuganni makes the five letters the arrow for the hunt in the grove where sun and moon have gone.

source_issues: 1505 line 1 and 4 read தங்காயம் / தங்காயந், a word not found in the dictionaries; probably a corrupt plant name.
1503 lines 2 and 3 differ only in வளைபரப்பி / வலைபரப்பி; one is probably a slip for the other.
1504 line 2 reads பாமவலி, probably for பாபவலி.
